afterword.heading: Afterword
afterword.attribution: The essay below is the kaisetsu (commentary-afterword) that the literary critic Musashino Jiro contributed to the 1987 Kobunsha bunko edition of the novel. It is reproduced here in translation as that edition's own critical appreciation of the book and its author; it is not part of Murayama's novel. Where it quotes the novel, the wording follows the present translation, and the internal dates it gives ("this month," "this year") are those of the novel's original serialization in 1963 and 1964.

blocks.text: The Ishikawa Goemon we picture, the hero of The Stealthy Ones, is after all the Goemon of legend: the great thief the age has rarely matched, the Goemon who steps onto the kabuki stage as gorgeous as a color woodblock print. At the Tokyo Kabuki-za in November 1987, one of the plays on the evening bill was Sanmon Gosan no Kiri, in which this Goemon appears; so it is only natural that the image we carry of him should settle, once again, on the master thief.

On the wall of the theater's ground-floor lobby there hangs a rare thing, and it is a pleasure to stop and look at it: a great tapestry woven from a painting of this splendid Goemon of Sanmon Gosan no Kiri, a picture the master painter Nabei Katsuyuki made, modeled on the Goemon of the late Jitsukawa Enjaku. It shows him seated atop the gate-tower of the Nanzen-ji, a hundred-day wig on his head, a thick padded gown thrown over his shoulders, a long pipe in his right hand. You half seem to hear, drifting up from somewhere, his famous line: 'A glorious view, a glorious view! To reckon the prospect of spring worth a thousand in gold at a single glance is to price it cheap, too cheap; to my eye it is worth ten thousand ryo at a glance, ten thousand upon ten thousand. Ah, what a soft and radiant prospect it is.'
Of this famous play the author himself writes, in the novel:

Of this first meeting of Hideyoshi and Goemon, Namiki Gohei wrote, a hundred and ninety-seven years later, in a kabuki play: the famous Kinmon Gosan no Kiri, in whose second act, second scene, the two are made to meet at the mountain gate of the Nanzen-ji. The scene was so great a hit that it was later cut loose to stand on its own, its title changed to Sanmon Gosan no Kiri, and has been played over and over. The late Enjaku made it the crowning role of his life; and this very month, September of 1963, at the Shin-Kabuki-za in Osaka, the third Enjaku plays it in the art his father handed down.
And again:

Why has this one scene gone on living a hundred and eighty-five years, ever since it was first put on in the fourth month of An'ei 7, in the day of the tenth shogun, Ieharu, at the Kado theater in Osaka, the present Dotonbori Kadoza? Because the wildly fanciful conceit satisfies the curiosity of the house: the great thief declaiming atop the grand gate, the cherries in full bloom below him, face to face with Hideyoshi, the man who would go on to take the realm, and to put Goemon to the cruel death of the cauldron.

That the author should take the play apart in this way is the more absorbing because he is himself a man of the theater: playwright, director, stage-designer. And it is his achievement, above all, to have taken this Goemon whom we so firmly picture as the great thief and brought him on as something altogether new, as a shinobi, a ninja, overturning everything we thought we knew. That is what Murayama Tomoyoshi did in the great five-part work The Stealthy Ones.

The stretch from October 1962, when the first part of The Stealthy Ones was first published, to about March 1965, when the second part appeared, was the very time when the ninja story, the ninpo tale, was booming in popular letters, in the field of historical fiction. The many such tales turned out one after another by popular writers, Yamada Futaro, Gomi Yasusuke, Shibata Renzaburo, and the rest, met with explosive success and were widely read.

Before the war, the tales of the ninjutsu-wielders, the stories of Sarutobi Sasuke, Kirigakure Saizo, and their like, had been a staple of the Tachikawa Bunko booklets and of the kodan storytellers, and were loved by ordinary people. After the war, in the world of historical fiction, ninjutsu turned into ninpo and reappeared in an entirely new dress: this was ninpo fiction. The new ninja stories of Yamada Futaro and others were marked by wildly inventive plotting, above all the outlandish tales of Yamada Futaro himself, so well received that they came to be called 'Futaro ninpo,' and were steeped, for the most part, in the flavor of the old historical-adventure romance.

It was into this vogue for ninja fiction that Murayama Tomoyoshi's The Stealthy Ones was launched, and its realistic rendering of the ninja's craft won it instant popularity and the notice of a great many readers. The author of this large work, Murayama Tomoyoshi, was a pillar of the left-wing shingeki, the new theater: a leading figure in the prewar productions of the Shinkyo Gekidan, and after the war, from the late 1940s on, a busy and well-known man of the theater who directed such new-theater pieces as Before the Dawn, The Lower Depths, and Ishikari-gawa. That such a man (he died in 1977, at seventy-six) should have written and published a ninja novel, and by it wholly overturned the ordinary image of Ishikawa Goemon, is a most interesting thing, and one that, I think, will keep its place in the history of postwar historical fiction.

When the first part of the novel appeared and caught the public, it was at once made into a film, at the Daiei Kyoto studio, in 1962. Directed by Yamamoto Satsuo, with a cast headed by Ichikawa Raizo and Ito Yunosuke, it succeeded as an unusual kind of period film and was warmly received. Ichikawa Raizo played Ishikawa Goemon, and Ito Yunosuke gave a fine double turn as both Fujibayashi Nagato-no-kami and Momochi Sandayu. The next year, 1963, again at the Daiei Kyoto studio, a sequel, Zoku Shinobi no mono, was filmed, another well-made period picture, with Raizo once more as Goemon and Wakayama Tomisaburo as Oda Nobunaga, made by the same staff. The success of these two period films, Shinobi no mono and its sequel, may be said to have created a new image of Ishikawa Goemon; and that they were shot not in color but in the tones of black and white suited the ninja film well. Shinobi no mono stands today as one of the representative works of Ichikawa Raizo, who died young.

Now, the story of the second part of The Stealthy Ones begins at the end of the third month of Tensho 10, that is, 1582. The opening describes a scene in which Tamo, a beggar-woman newly come to the capital, visits the Nanban-ji, the Christians' church; and the great temple that stands facing that church is Honno-ji, the head temple of the Hokke sect. That Oda Nobunaga would meet his death at this Honno-ji, in the sudden assault of Akechi Mitsuhide's revolt, is a famous event of history; and the way the Honno-ji Incident gives rise to the ascent of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and to the whole train of well-known Sengoku upheavals, is drawn out in this book too, in the form of a historical novel.

This was Honno-ji itself, the head temple of the Hokke sect. That within three short months history would swing on its hinge here, with this very place for a stage, Tamo of course had no way of guessing.

Familiar as these turns of history are, the book has, as a mark all Murayama's own, a wealth of meticulous research strewn through it, and that is part of its interest. There is more. Set into the narrative, quite apart from the story proper, are passages about the theater that only this author could have written, and they are among the most absorbing things in it. For instance:

This November—1964—I am directing one piece in the Shinkokugeki's run at the Meijiza, and for the rehearsals I came yesterday, the sixteenth of October, to Kokura in Kyushu. The company is playing at the Kokura Civic Hall, so we rehearse each morning from nine until noon, half an hour before the curtain. We were to have rehearsed late at night after the show, but no one would lend us a hall at that hour, and so it fell to the morning.

Such interpolations strike me as especially fascinating. In Tensho 12 (1584), and on into Tensho 13, Hideyoshi made a soaring, meteoric advance: raised to Chancellor of the Realm, granted the surname Toyotomi, he became the supreme power in the land. Meanwhile, when Goemon's one son, Goichi, was seven, Hideyoshi's own beloved child Tsurumatsu died of illness. The scene in which Goemon, hearing of it, shouts his savage delight,

Serves you right, Hideyoshi. Didn't you kill this boy's mother, and all but kill the boy as well? There's your judgment from Heaven, plain as day! Look here—my Goichi is growing up fine and strong! Beaten, are you? Does it gall you? Damn you, Hideyoshi!

gives powerful expression to Goemon's hatred of Hideyoshi. The final highlight comes when Goemon, bent on killing the Taiko Hideyoshi as he visits the Lady Yodo at Yodo Castle, works his way with great pains almost to the very bedchamber, only to be taken at last by the guard-captain Hattori Hanzo and his men.

He is then put, on the twenty-fourth day of the eighth month of Bunroku 3, that is, 1594, to the cruel death of the cauldron, at the execution ground of Sanjo-gawara in Kyoto. And since the Goemon best known to us is the Goemon of that Nanzen-ji gate-tower and of his end in the boiling cauldron, to read on to this closing passage is to be moved indeed. Taking for his hero Ishikawa Goemon, a legendary figure who flourished at the height of Hideyoshi's power, and whose very dates of birth and death are, historically, not clearly known, the author has built a full-dress Sengoku historical novel; and this book may fairly be called Murayama Tomoyoshi's representative work in the field of the novel.
One thing more. There is also this remark in the text:
And this year, 1964, in January, at the Toshi Center Hall, the Tokyo Geijutsu-za staged my own Goemon Kamairi.
so that here too, learning that the book has been made into a play from the author's own hand and put upon the stage, one feels, to the very end, a keen and lively interest.
